newsitem.title: BELARUS: World Bank official slams slow Belarus reforms. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: World Bank official slams slow Belarus reforms. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]

text.p: Reforms in Belarus have gone backwards, state interference has increased and the former Soviet republic could take as long as a decade to recover, a World Bank official said on Tuesday.

Christopher Willoughby, summing up his four years at the helm of the World Bank's Belarus office, did not mention President Alexander Lukashenko by name but made clear the leadership was at least partly to blame.
Lukashenko, who has tight control of all branches of power, has been repeatedly criticised in the West for his increasingly authoritarian rule and apparent reluctance to reform.

"The main obstacle on the path to reform is on the political level and in public opinion. It is hard to say to what extent this is the people's opinion and to what extent that of the leadership they have elected," Willoughby told a news conference.

He said economic restructuring had been in reverse since the second half of 1995, especially in the financial sector. "In October 1995 it became clear, and with every month it gets clearer, that the course is changing. Since then we have not been talking about serious World Bank credits.
"I am struck by the fear of the result of reforms in Belarus, liberalisation of the currency market and a repeat of the Russian privatisation experience," he added.

Belarus has been seeking ever closer economic and political ties with neighbouring Russia under Lukashenko who was elected in July 1994 -- but Willoughby said the country of 10 million had to understand that it could make decisions independently.
"This country's main resource is human -- highly-educated and qualified specialists. They must only be freed... State interference in all spheres is strengthening," he said.

"This is why reforms in Belarus have not worked out as they have in Poland, the Baltic states, as we hope they will work out in two to three years in Russia. For this Belarus will need maybe a year, maybe five, 10 or more years," he added.
Belarus has tightened controls on banks, businesses and the currency market while prices have been kept artificially low.
But Willoughby said the Bank, which is moving management of its Minsk operations to neighbouring Ukraine as part of restructuring, would keep working with Belarus.
A $10-$15 million energy conservation credit would be considered by a Bank delegation in mid-July -- though even that would be frozen if reforms were reversed further, he added.

He said Belarus, which has received $170 million (corrects from $710 million) from the Bank since the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991, was the only member of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) not to have received credits from the Bank in the last three years.
"The situation in Belarus is worse than it was two years ago. Backwards steps have been taken in state regulation in all spheres, including prices," he said.

Willoughby said increases in gross domestic product (GDP) did not tell the whole story as they were accompanied by high inflation and warned financial destabilisation would result if the economic course did not change.
He said GDP grew by 2.6 percent last year from 1995 and 10 percent from January to March compared to the same 1996 period.
Average monthly inflation between January and May this year was 6.1 percent -- despite the 2.0 percent average decreed by Lukashenko in the country's economic programme.

Willoughby said subsidised credits to the building sector had contributed to the rise in output. "This growth was achieved only because of administrative measures and cannot be supported by a growth in GDP in the next few years".
